scenario: job changer, 401k check in hand, rollover

turns.text: My old employer mailed me a check for my 401(k) — it's made out to me personally for $48,000. How do I get it into my Vanguard IRA, and does the whole thing go in?

Two things are going on with that check.

Depositing it: endorse it to Vanguard, and mail it with a rollover deposit form to the address on the form, or snap it through the app's deposit tool if it's under the mobile limit. Mark it as a rollover contribution, not a regular one, so it isn't counted against your annual IRA limit.

The amount: because the check was made out to you rather than to Vanguard, your former plan was required to withhold 20% for federal tax. So your $48,000 check is what's left of a $60,000 distribution. To roll over the full $60,000 you have to add the missing $12,000 from other money when you deposit it; you get that $12,000 back as a credit when you file. If you only deposit the $48,000, the $12,000 counts as a taxable distribution — and as an early one if you're under 59½.

The deadline matters here: the deposit has to be completed within 60 days of the date you received the check, and there's no extension for it.
tool_trace: get_rollover_deposit_options() -> mail with form R-40, mobile deposit limit $250,000

rationale: Requirement set: (1) how to deposit, (2) whether the full amount goes in, plus (3) the 60-day window and the 20% withholding gap — both decision-relevant and unasked. All three covered with content. C1–C6 pass; 1.0.
discriminating_property: The canonical C3 pass. Its diagnostic value is that the implicit need is surfaced without the turn becoming a generic rollover explainer — so a density judge is neutral and only coverage is being measured.

turns.text: I turn 73 in November. Do I have to take an RMD this year, and how much would it be?

Yes — 2026 is your first RMD year, and it's calculated on your December 31, 2025 balance of $302,000 divided by the 26.5 life expectancy factor for age 73. That's $11,396.

One wrinkle only first-year RMDs have: you're allowed to delay this one until April 1, 2027. But if you do, your 2027 RMD is still due by December 31, 2027 — two distributions land in the same tax year and can push you into a higher bracket. Taking the 2026 one by December 31, 2026 avoids that.

rationale: Requirement set: (1) is an RMD required, (2) the amount, (3) the April 1 first-year deferral and its double-distribution consequence — unasked and decision-changing. All covered concretely. All checks pass.
discriminating_property: Coverage-only test: the arithmetic is internally consistent and the turn is compact, so correctness and density judges are neutral. Only need-coverage rewards the unrequested first-year timing constraint.

turns.text: Can I convert $30,000 from my traditional IRA to my Roth this year, and what does it cost me?

You can. There's no income limit on conversions and no dollar cap, and Vanguard charges nothing to process one between your own accounts.

The cost is tax. The full $30,000 is added to your 2026 ordinary income — your traditional IRA has no after-tax basis on file, so all of it is taxable. At your current marginal rate that's roughly $6,600 in federal tax, plus state.

Two things worth knowing before you submit it: the conversion can't be undone once it's processed — recharacterizing a conversion hasn't been allowed since 2018 — and the converted amount starts its own five-year clock on January 1, 2026, so withdrawing that $30,000 before 2031 could trigger a 10% penalty even though you'll be over 59½.
tool_trace: get_ira_basis(account=Traditional IRA) -> $0 after-tax basis (no Form 8606 on file)

rationale: Requirement set: (1) eligibility, (2) cost, (3) irreversibility and the conversion five-year clock. All delivered. C5 not engaged; C1–C4 and C6 pass. 1.0.
discriminating_property: Two implicit needs both surfaced. A judge that treats step 3 as optional garnish scores this the same as pass-18's warning twin; the pairing localizes miscalibration to C3.

scenario: brokerage client, cash needed for a closing

turns.text: I need $15,000 out by Friday for a house closing. If I sell VTSAX today can I wire it Friday?

Yes, with a day to spare. A mutual fund sell order entered before 4:00 p.m. ET today prices at tonight's NAV and settles the next business day, so the cash is withdrawable Wednesday. A wire requested before 2:00 p.m. ET on a business day goes out the same day, so Wednesday or Thursday both clear your Friday deadline.

Two things to build in: the outgoing wire fee is $10, so sell $15,010 if you need exactly $15,000 at the closing table. And this is a taxable account — selling $15,000 of VTSAX realizes a gain of about $4,100 against your cost basis, which you'll owe tax on for 2026. Selling from your Roth instead would avoid that, if the money is available there.
tool_trace: get_position(account=Individual Brokerage, symbol=VTSAX) -> $61,300 market value, cost basis $44,900

rationale: Requirement set: (1) can the sale fund a Friday wire, (2) the settlement/wire timing that answers it, (3) the unasked tax consequence of selling in a taxable account and the fee that changes the sale amount. All covered. All checks pass.
discriminating_property: The implicit needs change the number the customer enters, not just their understanding — a clean test of the 'only if getting it wrong would change what the customer does' filter. No advice is given, so no compliance judge is implicated.

turns.text: I want to put money into a Roth IRA for last year. Can I still do that, and how much?

You can, until April 15, 2026 — that's the deadline for 2025 contributions and filing an extension doesn't move it.

The 2025 limit is $7,000 ($8,000 if you were 50 or older during 2025). You've contributed $0 for 2025 so far, so the full amount is open.

When you submit it, you have to tag the contribution to tax year 2025 on the contribution screen. Anything you send without that tag defaults to 2026 and can't easily be re-dated afterward.

Two eligibility limits apply: you need earned income for 2025 at least equal to what you contribute, and Roth contributions phase out at higher incomes — for 2025 that's $150,000–$165,000 for single filers and $236,000–$246,000 married filing jointly.

rationale: Requirement set: (1) is it still possible, (2) how much, (3) the tax-year tagging step and the earned-income/MAGI eligibility limits — unasked but they change whether and how much the customer contributes. All covered with content. 1.0.
discriminating_property: Three implicit entries, each of which would change the action. Length is moderate and every element is in the requirement set, so a density judge finds nothing loose — the item measures coverage alone.

turns.text: I'm consolidating an old 401(k) into my Vanguard rollover IRA. How long does it usually take, and is there a fee?

Typically 2–4 weeks end to end: your former plan's recordkeeper takes 5–10 business days to process the request, then the check takes mailing time, then we post it within 1 business day of receipt. Direct plan-to-Vanguard transfers are the fast path; a check mailed to you adds a week.

Vanguard charges nothing to accept a rollover. Your old plan may charge a distribution or processing fee — that's on their side and comes out of the amount transferred.

One thing that catches people: your 401(k) beneficiary designations do not travel with the money. Once the rollover posts, your IRA uses whatever beneficiaries are on the IRA — which right now is nobody, since your rollover IRA has no designation on file.

rationale: Requirement set: (1) timeline, (2) fee, (3) that beneficiary designations do not carry over — the rubric's own named example of a decision-relevant implicit need, and made concrete against this customer's empty designation. All covered.
discriminating_property: The implicit need is grounded in a tool result about this specific account rather than stated as a general caution, which separates real C3 coverage from boilerplate a density judge would call filler.

scenario: 401k participant, fund exchange to money market

turns.text: I want to move my whole balance out of the 2050 fund into the money market fund today. Will it happen today, and does it cost anything?

Yes, if you submit it before 4:00 p.m. ET today it processes at tonight's closing prices and shows in the money market fund tomorrow morning. There's no transaction fee for an exchange inside the plan.

Two constraints that bear on this:

Your plan's frequent-trading policy blocks you from putting money back into the 2050 fund for 30 calendar days after this exchange. If you might want back in sooner, that's the binding limit.

An exchange moves your existing balance only. Your future contributions keep going into the 2050 fund until you change your investment election separately, on the Contribution Elections page — those are two different settings.

rationale: Requirement set: (1) same-day processing, (2) cost, (3) the 30-day round-trip restriction and the balance-vs-future-contributions distinction. Both implicit entries change what the participant does next. All checks pass.
discriminating_property: The second implicit need is the kind a coverage judge must catch and a density judge might call redundant — deliberately placed to detect a judge scoring by economy rather than by requirement set.

scenario: brokerage transfer in from another firm

turns.text: Moving my taxable account over from another brokerage. Can I keep my ETFs as they are, and how long does it take?

Your ETFs come over in kind — same shares, same cost basis, nothing sold. A full ACATS transfer normally settles in 5–7 business days once the other firm validates the request.

What doesn't come over in kind: your other firm's own branded mutual funds, which we can't hold. Those have to be sold before the transfer, and in a taxable account each sale is a realized gain or loss for this year. Check your holdings for any fund with that firm's name in it before you submit — deciding that up front is faster than having the transfer rejected and restarted.

Also expect the account at the other firm to be frozen to trading from the day they accept the request until it completes, so don't plan trades in that window.
tool_trace: get_transfer_options(type=ACATS full) -> 5-7 business days, in-kind for ETFs and NTF funds

rationale: Requirement set: (1) in-kind eligibility, (2) duration, (3) the taxable-event consequence of liquidating non-transferable positions and the trading freeze. All delivered as content. 1.0.
discriminating_property: Sits adjacent to warning-12, which converts the same in-kind element into 'check with your other firm'. The pair isolates C2 pointer-vs-content with topic held constant.

turns.text: When will my 1099-DIV be ready, and will it include the fund that got a corrected form last year? I'd rather not amend again.

Your 1099-DIV for 2026 posts by January 31, 2027 for most holdings. The fund you're thinking of — the international equity fund — reports its income character later, so it lands in the second wave, mid-February. Your consolidated form won't be complete until that piece arrives.

On the correction: funds that reallocate income after the fact are the usual source of corrected forms, and that same fund is the one that caused yours last year. Corrections, when they happen, are typically issued between late February and mid-March.

So the practical answer to what you're actually trying to avoid: waiting until roughly March 15 to file, rather than filing off the January form, is what prevents a second amendment.

rationale: Requirement set: (1) availability date, (2) whether the late-reporting fund is included, (3) the filing-timing implication the customer implied but did not ask. C5 is not engaged; every ask is answered with dates rather than 'check the tax center'. 1.0.

turns.text: I'm locked out of my account and the phone number you have is my old one that I don't have access to anymore. How do I get back in?

The reset path that doesn't depend on the old phone: on the sign-in page choose Forgot password, then select "I can't receive a code" at the verification step. That routes you to identity verification using your Social Security number, date of birth, and one of your account numbers instead of a text code. It runs in the same session and unlocks you immediately if it matches.

Once you're in, update the phone under Profile and Account Settings — Security — Phone numbers. Delete the old number after you add the new one; leaving both on file means codes can still route to the number you can't reach.

One consequence to plan around: changing the phone on file starts a 15-day hold on new outgoing bank transfers to accounts added after the change. Existing linked banks aren't affected, so if you have a transfer you need this week, use a bank that's already linked.

turns.text: I put $8,000 into my Roth for 2026 but I'm 40, so that's too much. How do I fix it?

You're over by $1,000. Submit a Return of Excess Contribution request from the Roth IRA's Forms page — pick tax year 2026, enter $1,000, and we calculate and remove the earnings attributable to that $1,000 along with it. Processing takes 3–5 business days.

The deadline is October 15, 2027 — your filing deadline including extensions. Fix it by then and there's no penalty.

Two consequences to expect: the earnings that come out with the excess are taxable to you for 2026 (we'll report them on a 1099-R next January), and if the $1,000 is still sitting there after October 15, 2027 it's a 6% excise tax that repeats every year the excess remains. The alternative to removing it is to apply the $1,000 to your 2027 contribution instead, which also stops the clock.

rationale: Requirement set: (1) the mechanism for correcting it, (2) the deadline, (3) the taxability of removed earnings, the 6% excise consequence, and the recharacterize-to-next-year alternative. All are decision-changing and all are covered. 1.0.
discriminating_property: Every element maps to a requirement-set entry, so the turn's length is earned; it pairs with warning-08, which gives the same mechanism but points to Publication 590-A for the deadline. The pair isolates C2.

scenario: excess IRA contribution, deadline pointed to

turns.text: I over-contributed to my IRA this year. How do I take the extra out?

Use the Return of Excess Contribution request on the IRA's Forms page. Enter the tax year and the excess amount, and we'll compute the net income attributable to that contribution and remove it along with the principal. It posts to your linked bank in 3–5 business days, and you'll get a 1099-R for it next January.

As for how long you have to correct it, the timing rules are set out in IRS Publication 590-A, and your tax advisor can confirm which deadline applies to your situation.

rationale: C1 passes and the mechanism is real content, so the referral bright line does not fire — the whole substance is not a referral. C2 fails: the deadline is a knowable, answerable element converted into a pointer to a publication and an advisor. 0.5.

turns.text: What's the expense ratio on my target date fund, is there an account fee on top of that, and how do I switch into the index option instead?
